$$\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q):=T_k(V)/J_Q.$$

## Definition

Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Riemannian manifold of even dimension $2m$, and let $V=V^+\oplus V^-$ be a finite-rank smooth complex vector bundle with a Hermitian metric linear in its first variable. Write $\mathrm{Cl}_{\mathbb C}(T^*M,-g)$ for the complex Clifford bundle generated by cotangent vectors with relation $\xi\eta+\eta\xi=-2g^{-1}(\xi,\eta)$. A **graded Hermitian Clifford action** is a smooth real-linear map $c:T^*M\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ such that $c(\xi)^*=-c(\xi)$, $c(\xi)V^\pm\subseteq V^\mp$, and $c(\xi)c(\eta)+c(\eta)c(\xi)=-2g^{-1}(\xi,\eta)I$. It extends complex-linearly to the complex Clifford bundle.

A **graded Hermitian Clifford connection** is a unitary connection $\nabla^V$ preserving $V^\pm$ and satisfying
$$\nabla^V_X(c(\xi)v)=c(\nabla^{LC}_X\xi)v+c(\xi)\nabla^V_Xv$$
for smooth $X,\xi,v$, where $\nabla^{LC}$ is the Levi–Civita connection. In a local orthonormal coframe $(e^i)$ define
$$D_Vv=\sum_i c(e^i)\nabla^V_{e_i}v.$$
The operator is odd, so its chiral part is $D_V^+:C^\infty(V^+)\to C^\infty(V^-)$. The formula's frame independence, formal symmetry on closed $M$, and global bundle well-definedness are proved in [[lem-geometric-dirac-operator-is-well-defined]]. A domain and index are assigned only under the compact hypotheses of later items.

## Statement

For a supplied graded Hermitian Clifford module and compatible connection as in [[def-graded-hermitian-clifford-module-and-geometric-dirac]], the local expression $D_V=\sum_i c(e^i)\nabla^V_{e_i}$ is independent of oriented orthonormal frame, is a smooth globally defined first-order differential operator, and is formally symmetric on a closed $M$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A smooth oriented Riemannian manifold, a graded Hermitian Clifford module $V$, and a supplied graded Hermitian Clifford connection $\nabla^V$.

[F1] The Clifford relation, odd action and skew-Hermitian condition are exactly those in [[def-graded-hermitian-clifford-module-and-geometric-dirac]].

[F2] A Clifford connection obeys $\nabla^V_X(c(\xi)v)=c(\nabla^{LC}_X\xi)v+c(\xi)\nabla^V_Xv$ ([[def-graded-hermitian-clifford-module-and-geometric-dirac]], [[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]]).

[F3] On a closed Riemannian manifold, the integral of the divergence of a smooth vector field is zero under countable choice ([[thm-riemannian-divergence-theorem]]).

[A1] This proof uses only $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through [F3]; it is declared in [[def-countable-choice]].

## Proof

**Given:** The stated module, connection and closed manifold.

1.1 On an overlap let $e'_i=\sum_j a_{ij}e_j$ be a change of oriented orthonormal frame, so $A=(a_{ij})$ is orthogonal. The dual coframe changes by the same orthogonal coefficient matrix with the corresponding inverse convention, while $\nabla_{e'_i}=\sum_k a_{ik}\nabla_{e_k}$. Therefore $\sum_i c(e'^i)\nabla_{e'_i}=\sum_{i,j,k}a_{ij}a_{ik}c(e^j)\nabla_{e_k}=\sum_jc(e^j)\nabla_{e_j}$ by $\sum_i a_{ij}a_{ik}=\delta_{jk}$. Each chart expression has smooth coefficients, and these overlap equalities glue them to one global first-order operator. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Define the complex vector field $Y=\sum_i\langle c(e^i)u,v\rangle e_i$ for smooth sections $u,v$. At any chosen point take a local orthonormal frame with $\nabla^{LC}e_i=0$ there. Using [F2], metric compatibility and $\nabla e_i=0$ at that point gives $\operatorname{div}Y=\langle D_Vu,v\rangle-\langle u,D_Vv\rangle$: the second term has this sign because $c(e^i)^*=-c(e^i)$ and the Hermitian pairing is linear in its first variable. Since this is a pointwise identity independent of the chosen normal frame, it holds globally. Apply [F3] to real and imaginary parts of $Y$ and integrate to get $\int_M\langle D_Vu,v\rangle=\int_M\langle u,D_Vv\rangle$. Thus $D_V$ is formally symmetric. Oddness follows termwise because each $c(e^i)$ is odd and $\nabla$ preserves grading. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1] ∎

## Definition

Let $\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ be the complex field, whose elements have unique coordinates $z=a+b\mathrm i$ ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Write $\bar z=a-b\mathrm i$ for complex conjugation ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). Let

$$
\mathbb H=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}z&w\\-\bar w&\bar z\end{pmatrix}:z,w\in\mathbb C\right\}\subseteq M_2(\mathbb C)
$$

with addition and multiplication inherited from matrices. This is a real associative algebra: multiplying the matrices with parameters $(z,w)$ and $(z',w')$ gives the matrix with parameters $(zz'-w\bar w',\,zw'+w\bar z')$. Its real basis is $1,i,j,k$, where
$i=\operatorname{diag}(\mathrm i,-\mathrm i)$, $j=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $k=ij$; these satisfy $i^2=j^2=k^2=-1$, $ij=k$, $jk=i$, $ki=j$, and reversing any of the last three products changes its sign.

For $D\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C,\mathbb H\}$ and a positive integer $m$, $M_m(D)$ is the associative algebra of $m\times m$ matrices with entries in $D$. The direct sum $A\oplus B$ of algebras has componentwise addition and multiplication. The opposite algebra $D^{\mathrm{op}}$ has the same addition and unit as $D$, with multiplication $d\cdot_{\mathrm{op}}e:=ed$. A left module is **simple** when it is nonzero and has no proper nonzero submodule ([[def-simple-module]]). For a simple left $M_m(D)$-module $S$, its coefficient type is $D$ when $\operatorname{End}_{M_m(D)}(S)\cong D^{\mathrm{op}}$; the classification theorem below proves the matrix-algebra cases used on this page.

## Definition

$$\Gamma(V,B)=\{x\in\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)^\times:\alpha(x)v x^{-1}\in V\text{ for every }v\in V\},\qquad \rho_x(v)=\alpha(x)v x^{-1}.$$

$$\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(V,Q)=\operatorname{Pin}(V,Q)\cap\mathrm{Cl}^0,\qquad \operatorname{Spin}_{N=1}(V,Q)=\{x\in\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(V,Q):N(x)=1\}.$$

## Definition

Let $k$ be a field with $\operatorname{char}(k)\ne2$, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space, and let $B:V\times V\to k$ be a symmetric bilinear form, not necessarily nondegenerate. Put $Q(v)=B(v,v)$. Write $T_k(V)$ for the tensor algebra and $j:V\to T_k(V)$ for its degree-one inclusion ([[def-tensor-algebra-of-a-vector-space]]). For each $v\in V$, set $r_v=j(v)j(v)-Q(v)1$ and let $J_Q$ be the intersection of all two-sided ideals of $T_k(V)$ containing every $r_v$ ([[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]]). This family is nonempty because it contains $T_k(V)$, and its intersection is a two-sided ideal; thus $J_Q$ is the smallest such ideal.

Define the **universal Clifford algebra** with the plus-$Q$ convention by

$$\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q):=T_k(V)/J_Q.$$

The quotient operations are induced from $T_k(V)$; the two-sided ideal condition makes multiplication of cosets well defined. Let $q_Q:T_k(V)\to\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q)$ be the quotient map, put $i_Q=q_Q\circ j$, and write $\bar v=i_Q(v)$. The defining relation is $\bar v^{\,2}=Q(v)1$. In this pair, $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ abbreviates $\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q)$ after this sign convention has been fixed. No nondegeneracy assumption is imposed.

## Definition

Let $V\to X$ be a finite-rank Euclidean real vector bundle and put $C(V)=\mathrm{Cl}(V,-\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$, so each vector $v$ acts with square $-\lVert v\rVert^2$. An **ungraded** $C(V)$-module bundle is a finite-rank real vector bundle with continuous fiberwise unital Clifford action. Write $K_{C(V)}(X)$ for the Grothendieck group of their direct-sum monoid.

A **graded** $C(V)$-module bundle is a module $\Lambda=\Lambda^0\oplus\Lambda^1$ whose action satisfies $C(V)^i\Lambda^j\subseteq\Lambda^{i+j}$, with indices modulo two. The same convention gives $M_n$ for the negative Clifford algebra $C_n=\mathrm{Cl}_{0,n}$ over a point. The rank-$4m$ volume Thom theorem uses the former, whereas ABS uses a restriction quotient of the latter.

## Definition

Let $k$ be a field. A $\mathbb Z/2$-graded $k$-vector space is a direct sum $A=A^0\oplus A^1$; a homogeneous element $a\in A^i$ has parity $|a|=i\in\{0,1\}$. A $\mathbb Z/2$-graded unital associative $k$-algebra is such a space with $1\in A^0$ and $A^iA^j\subseteq A^{i+j\pmod 2}$. A graded left module is a module $M=M^0\oplus M^1$ satisfying $A^iM^j\subseteq M^{i+j\pmod 2}$. A graded submodule is an $A$-submodule $N=N^0\oplus N^1$; a graded-simple module is nonzero and has no proper nonzero graded submodule. An isomorphism of graded modules preserves both parity components.

For graded algebras $A,B$, their graded tensor product $A\widehat\otimes_k B$ has underlying vector space $A\otimes_kB$, parity $(A\widehat\otimes B)^r=\bigoplus_{i+j=r}A^i\otimes_kB^j$, and multiplication

$$
(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=(-1)^{|b||a'|}(aa'\otimes bb')
$$

for homogeneous factors, extended by the finite sum

$$
\sum_{i,j,r,s\in\{0,1\}}(-1)^{jr}(a_i a'_r\otimes b_j b'_s),\qquad a=\sum_i a_i,\ b=\sum_j b_j,\ a'=\sum_r a'_r,\ b'=\sum_s b'_s.
$$

Each parity projection is linear, so this formula is $k$-multilinear in the four inputs and therefore defines a multiplication on $(A\otimes_kB)\times(A\otimes_kB)$ by [[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The unit is $1_A\otimes1_B$. For three homogeneous tensors, both associative bracketings contribute the sign exponent $|b||a'|+|b||a''|+|b'||a''|$, so the multiplication is associative.

## Statement

Let $k,V,B,Q$ be as in [[def-clifford-algebra-of-a-quadratic-space]], and let $\bar v=i_Q(v)$. Then

$$\bar v\bar w+\bar w\bar v=2B(v,w)1$$

consumer_facts_or_definition: [F2] Orthogonal vectors anticommute under the polarized Clifford relation ([[lem-clifford-polarized-relations]]).
consumer_use_steps: 1.1 In an oriented orthonormal frame the generators anticommute and each has square $-1$. Reversing the product order takes $n(n-1)/2=2m(4m-1)$ swaps, an even number; multiplying the $n$ generator squares contributes $(-1)^{4m}=1$. Thus $\omega^2=1$. For any orthonormal frame, pairwise anticommutation makes the product equal to the alternating product $\operatorname{Alt}(v_1,\ldots,v_n)=\frac1{n!}\sum_\sigma\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)c(v_{\sigma(1)})\cdots c(v_{\sigma(n)})$. This is an alternating multilinear function of the frame vectors. An oriented orthogonal change has determinant $+1$, so it leaves this top alternating product unchanged. Hence $\omega$ is frame-independent and, in local frames, varies continuously. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 Moving any unit vector $v$ past the other $n-1$ orthogonal generators gives $\omega c(v)=(-1)^{n-1}c(v)\omega=-c(v)\omega$. If the module also has a parity grading, $\omega$ has even parity because $n$ is even, so it preserves $\Lambda^0$ and $\Lambda^1$. The continuous maps $p_\pm=(I\pm\omega)/2$ are idempotents with $p_+p_-=0$ and $p_++p_-=I$. In any local frame their matrix entries vary continuously, and the trace of an idempotent equals its rank, so each image rank is locally constant. At a point choose a basis of the image; applying $p_\pm$ to the same frame vectors remains independent on a neighborhood and spans the image there. Thus their images are complementary subbundles (graded when a parity grading is supplied). The anticommutation identity makes $c(v)$ interchange their images, and $c(v)^{-1}=-c(v)$ for $\lVert v\rVert=1$, so the interchange is an isomorphism. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

## Definition

Let $k$ be a field with $\operatorname{char}(k)\ne2$, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space, and let $B:V\times V\to k$ be a symmetric bilinear form, not necessarily nondegenerate. Put $Q(v)=B(v,v)$. Write $T_k(V)$ for the tensor algebra and $j:V\to T_k(V)$ for its degree-one inclusion ([[def-tensor-algebra-of-a-vector-space]]). For each $v\in V$, set $r_v=j(v)j(v)-Q(v)1$ and let $J_Q$ be the intersection of all two-sided ideals of $T_k(V)$ containing every $r_v$ ([[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]]). This family is nonempty because it contains $T_k(V)$, and its intersection is a two-sided ideal; thus $J_Q$ is the smallest such ideal.

Define the **universal Clifford algebra** with the plus-$Q$ convention by

$$\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q):=T_k(V)/J_Q.$$

The quotient operations are induced from $T_k(V)$; the two-sided ideal condition makes multiplication of cosets well defined. Let $q_Q:T_k(V)\to\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q)$ be the quotient map, put $i_Q=q_Q\circ j$, and write $\bar v=i_Q(v)$. The defining relation is $\bar v^{\,2}=Q(v)1$. In this pair, $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ abbreviates $\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q)$ after this sign convention has been fixed. No nondegeneracy assumption is imposed.
